At low tide the harbor looked like a room after its furniture had been carried away. Dark rectangles marked the resting places of boats, and narrow channels ran between them like passages left clear for guests. The windows of the old customs house reflected a sky that had not yet decided whether to brighten. Inside, the clock above the stairs had stopped at a quarter past six.

Mara placed a folded chart beside the ledger. The paper had belonged to Ellis, whose careful repairs could still be seen along its edges. Every tear had been backed with a thin strip of linen. A small brass weight held down the corner nearest the open window. Beyond the glass, water dripped steadily from the end of a broken gutter into a bucket full of leaves.

The building was due to become a public reading room before winter. There would be shelves where the inspection counter stood and a long table beneath the south windows. For now, dust lay on the boards in pale drifts. Mara worked around the heavier furniture, opening drawers one at a time and returning their contents in the same order. Nothing in the ledger explained why the last vessel had left without its bell.

By noon, the exposed mud had begun to shine. A child on the far quay dragged a stick along the railings, too distant for any sound to reach the customs house. Ellis had once drawn that quay with a different angle, before the outer wall collapsed. The old line remained beneath the new ink, faint but continuous, making an island of a place that was now joined to shore.

Mara turned the chart so that both versions faced the window. Under the changing light, a penciled path became visible between the warehouse and the landing steps. It ended at a square no larger than a fingernail. The square occupied the position of the missing bell tower. Outside, the returning tide touched the first mooring post. Mara left the chart open and went downstairs to find a measuring tape before the path disappeared beneath the water again.
